body.text: No great power of perception is needed to recognise that Josh Frydenberg would still like to be prime minister but hasn’t yet decided whether to run for preselection in Kooyong. As treasurer, he lost the seat to independent Monique Ryan in 2022 at the election that swept the Morrison government from office. As he has said several times, he still lives in, and enjoys strong ties within, the electorate.

Kooyong used to be prime Liberal realty, of course. It was the seat of Australia’s longest-serving prime minister, Robert Menzies (1934–66 in Kooyong, prime minister 1939–41 and 1949–66), and then Andrew Peacock, that charismatic and photogenic figure — at least in theory — who led the Coalition to two defeats (though they won the national two-party preferred vote at the second in 1990). Next was Petro Georgiou (1994–2010), self-styled progressive conscience of the party and hence press gallery favourite. As with many a party maverick, a chicken-and-egg question hovered: which came first, the independent streak or the lack of advancement into cabinet? (John Howard offered him a parliamentary secretary position in 1998, but he considered it beneath him.)

By contrast with Georgiou but like Peacock, Frydenberg rose pretty quickly through the ranks after his election in 2010. By 2013 he was in Tony Abbott’s ministry; he joined Malcolm Turnbull’s cabinet in 2015. But the Australian electorate was fragmenting, with both major parties shedding support and those once indomitable fortresses for future leaders, the party’s blue-ribbon seats, finally proved destructible. In 2022 Kooyong, along with five others, was swept away by teal independents.

In all six of those contests, the teal trailed the Liberal on primary votes. It was preferences, overwhelmingly flowing from Labor and Greens candidates, that catapulted them over the fifty-point mark. The trick was gathering enough alienated Liberal supporters to add to those left-of-centre votes. And it’s fair to say the chief driver of this swollen crossbench was the persona of prime minister Scott Morrison and his government’s sometimes boastful refusal to do much about global warming. (You could argue that Morrison’s much-rewatched 2017 parliamentary stunt with a lump of coal played an important part in both his elevation to the prime ministership the following year and the mass defection of teal voters four years later.)

The question of teal durability post-Morrison might appear to have been answered last year when all but one was returned and another joined their ranks, but it’s not that simple. Labor’s huge national two-party-preferred vote of 55.2 per cent, its biggest since 1943, played a part in at least the closer contests. The bigger the total left-of-centre vote, the more preferences flow to teals (including due to the influence of how-to-vote cards). In New South Wales the two-party-preferred swing to Labor was 3.9 points, and every sitting teal received a swing. In Victoria the swing to Labor was only 1.5 points and both teals lost ground. Zoe Daniel was defeated in Goldstein and Monique Ryan hung on by the narrowest margin. Had Amelia Hamer received 0.7 points more at Ryan’s expense she would have won. One point from Labor would have given her the seat, assuming the remaining Labor preferences flowed at the same rates.
This is no coincidence. Where Labor went swingwise, so went the teals.

(Readers will have noted I don’t here classify Zali Steggall, Rebekkah Sharkie and Helen Haines as teals. All were elected before 2022 and — apart from Steggall — don’t represent remotely tealish electorates. All three were easily re-elected, with bigger margins than any teal, in both 2022 and 2025.)

Over the last almost eighteen months the electoral landscape has dramatically transformed, and it’s to do with the huge increase in One Nation’s polled support. The Coalition has suffered more damage than Labor; One Nation support tends to increase with an electorate’s distance from a capital city’s central business district. We don’t know what it all will look like in another year and a half, but if we assume One Nation misses out on the two-candidate-preferred count in Kooyong in 2028 (and I reckon we can), its preferences will overwhelmingly favour the Liberal candidate (77 per cent of them flowed to Hamer last year).
So Kooyong was line-ball last year, and is certainly winnable for the Liberals next time.
(A recent DemosAU MRP actually gave the Libs a big 56 per cent two-party-preferred win in Kooyong, but MRPs are notoriously poor at estimating support for independents.)

Would Frydenberg make a good candidate — better than, say, Hamer? That’s not clear. He has name recognition and a ready-made personal vote, but is that personal vote positive or negative? Frydenberg doesn’t do subtlety. He has long had a tendency to play to the true believers: who can forget his repeated bagging of Victorian premier Dan Andrews during early Covid, culminating in a thundering parliamentary denunciation in late October 2020? It went down very well in the News Corp ecosphere, thrilling Coalition diehards everywhere, but Andrews, like all the state premiers, was still enjoying huge popularity. His surveyed satisfaction rating actually hit an all-time high from any pollster — 71 per cent in Roy Morgan — just weeks after Josh’s speech. Might the tirade have even damaged Frydenberg at the 2022 election?

Similarly, his somewhat obscene Bondi rant the day after last December’s massacre, placing responsibility squarely, personally, at the feet of Anthony Albanese, received wild acclaim from people who detest the prime minister but isn’t likely to have travelled well beyond the choir. Most voters didn’t think much of Albanese then, and even fewer do now, but that was too much. Playing to the base is brilliant for preselection; beyond that it can turn voters off.

In a similar vein, Josh recently announced that he spent too much money as treasurer during Covid (Liberal leader Angus Taylor later parroted the same line): red meat again for Sky After Dark aficionados, but is it something the voters want to hear? It certainly doesn’t heighten his economic credentials. (Morrison wouldn’t have enjoyed it, but he’s now used to the view of buses’ undercarriages thanks to former colleagues.)

There’s one more variable, on the downside, that Frydenberg should consider: the extreme likelihood of a change of state government next month. Victoria has been a relatively weak spot for federal Labor in recent Newspoll quarterlies, thanks in large part to the rather long-in-the-tooth, greatly unloved party in power. Last year’s relatively modest swing to the Albanese government in that state has been noted.
The removal of that dead weight should lift the Albanese government’s support in Victoria. And, as we know, what’s good for Labor at the ballot box tends to be good for teals. •
